samples.text:
The table shows how much water was used in Aldburgh city in 2004 and 2024, and the bar chart shows the level of the reservoir at the end of each seasons in 2024.

Overall, the total water consumption decreased and the reservoir was lowest in the summer.

In the table, homes used the most water in both years. It was 142 million litres per day in 2004 and 128 million litres in 2024. Industry used 96 million litres in 2004 but it dropped to 54 million litres, which is a big decrease. Leakage also fell from 61 to 33 million litres. However, commerce and offices was the only one that increased, from 38 to 45 million litres per day. So the total went down from 337 million to 260 million litres per day.

In the bar chart, the reservoir was 94% full at the end of winter, that was the highest level. Then it fell to 82% in spring and to 51% in summer. After summer it rised again to 67% in autumn, but it was still lower than in winter and spring.
samples.why: Short, basic overview · both visuals covered accurately, though with limited comparison · simple linking (However, So, Then) · repetitive vocabulary · errors in agreement, verb forms and relative pronouns.

samples.text:
The table compares the amount of water used for different purposes in Aldburgh in 2004 and 2024, while the bar chart shows how full the city's reservoir was at the end of each season in 2024.

Overall, total water consumption fell considerably over the twenty years, with most categories declining. The reservoir level was highest after winter and lowest after summer.

In 2004, Aldburgh consumed 337 million litres of water a day, but by 2024 this had dropped to 260 million. Homes remained the largest user, although their consumption decrease slightly from 142 to 128 million litres. The most significant fall was seen in industry, whose use fell by 42 million litres, from 96 to 54 million, and leakage was also reduced substantially, from 61 to 33 million litres. Commerce and offices was the only category to increase, rising from 38 to 45 million litres per day.

Turning to the reservoir, it was 94% full at the end of winter 2024. The level then declined to 82% by the end of spring and fell sharply to just 51% after summer, meaning that it was only around half full. By the end of autumn, it had partly recovered to 67% of capacity.
samples.why: Clear overview of consumption and seasonal pattern · key features highlighted, including the largest fall · logical paragraphs and good linkers · some less common vocabulary (capacity, substantially) · one minor verb slip.

samples.text:
The table details daily water consumption in Aldburgh by type of use in 2004 and 2024, and the bar chart shows the city's reservoir level at the end of each season in 2024.

The city's total water use fell markedly over the twenty years, mainly because of reductions in industrial demand and leakage. In 2024, the reservoir followed a clear seasonal cycle, being fullest after winter and most depleted after summer.

Total consumption dropped from 337 to 260 million litres per day, a reduction of 77 million litres. Industry and leakage together accounted for most of this decrease: industrial use fell from 96 to 54 million litres, and losses through leakage were cut from 61 to 33 million. Homes continued to be the largest consumer, although their use eased from 142 to 128 million litres. Commerce and offices bucked the overall trend, with consumption rising from 38 to 45 million litres.

The reservoir stood at 94% of capacity at the end of winter, slipping to 82% by the end of spring. It then dropped steeply over the summer, to just 51%, before partially recovering to 67% by the end of autumn.
samples.why: Well-structured overview that identifies what drove the fall in total use · figures selected and combined accurately · cohesion managed skilfully · precise vocabulary (depleted, bucked the trend, eased) · error-free, varied structures.
